paper_title: Beyond Benchmarks: Can Small Open-Weight Models Get Real Coding Work Done?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Making an open-weight language model generate text is not the same as making it finish coding work. This retrospective empirical systems experience report follows my engineering work from July to October 2026 across coding clients, model-specific serving recipes, vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, and MLX. Models behind a nominally compatible endpoint still differed in tool-call formatting, turn control, context behavior, cache reuse, and reliability. A served model, coherent text, executed tool calls, and code that passes independent behavioral checks proved to be distinct levels of progress. The evidence includes 4,165 coding-agent gateway turns from my own sessions, 623 debug jobs, and three separate delegation studies with hidden behavioral checks and a fixed Claude Opus 5.5 parent. Saved cold-prefix requests had a median time to first token of about 69.4 s, versus 2.8 s for high-reuse requests (observational). In a 45-trial study, direct coding passed 15/15 and delegation to a quantized Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B worker passed 12/15 and 14/15. On a second 15-task suite under a fixed artifact contract, the completed replacement cohort had 45/45 for direct coding and 12/45 for a Nemotron Cascade 2 worker (11 worker substitutions). Sixteen sessions stopped by a subscription limit before any model call were replaced; counting them as failures gives 37/45 and 8/45. A Qwen3-Coder worker passed 0/45. In both studies with a direct arm, direct coding had lower API list-price-equivalent frontier cost per verified success. A post-hoc diagnostic found that 19 of 36 artifacts rejected only for renamed parameters passed the hidden checks unchanged; they are not counted as successes. The contribution is an evidence-qualified account of serving, agent protocol, session continuity, artifact validation, and verification in practice. The studies are not pooled and do not rank models or runtimes.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Making an open-weight language model generate text is not the same as making it finish coding work. This retrospective empirical systems experience report follows my engineering work from July to October 2026 across coding clients, model-specific serving recipes, vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, and MLX. Models behind nominally compatible endpoint still differed in tool-call formatting, turn control, context behavior, cache reuse, and reliability. served model, coherent text, executed tool calls, and code that passes independent behavioral checks proved to be distinct levels of progress. The evidence includes 4,165 coding-agent gateway turns from my own sessions, 623 debug jobs, and three separate delegation studies with hidden behavioral checks and fixed Claude Opus 5.5 parent. Saved cold-prefix requests had median time to first token of about 69.4 s, versus 2.8 for high-reuse requests (observational). In 45-trial study, direct coding passed 15/15 and delegation to quantized Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B worker passed 12/15 and 14/15. On second 15-task suite under fixed artifact contract, the completed replacement cohort had 45/45 for direct coding and 12/45 for Nemotron Cascade 2 worker (11 worker substitutions). Sixteen sessions stopped by subscription limit before any model call were replaced; counting them as failures gives 37/45 and 8/45. Qwen3-Coder worker passed 0/45. In both studies with direct arm, direct coding had lower API list-price-equivalent frontier cost per verified success. post-hoc diagnostic found that 19 of 36 artifacts rejected only for renamed parameters passed the hidden checks unchanged; they are not counted as successes. The contribution is an evidence-qualified account of serving, agent protocol, session continuity, artifact validation, and verification in practice. The studies are not pooled and do not rank models or runtimes. Keywords: open-weight language models; coding agents; software engineering; inference systems; tool calling; KV caching; model serving; empirical experience report 1. Introduction: From Running Model to Finished Work An early question was broader than coding agents: could ordinary laptops pool their memory and computation to serve models too large for any one machine, without requiring specialized wired interconnect? imagined teammates, even in different locations, sharing access to more capable model instead of each developer needing enough memory to host it independently. initially expected that reaching larger model might improve the quality of coding assistance. The subsequent work 1 exposed second question: even if the distributed model could answer, could it support productive coding agent? It quickly became apparent that the model is running is very weak success criterion. checkpoint can load and answer questions yet fail when client asks it to inspect file, call tool, keep long session alive, or preserve repository contract. first tested that distributed idea with llama.cpp across laptops. Cloud serving began while was still experimenting with distributed inference on Macs. As sharded chat proved more usable than sharded coding-agent sessions, gradually made single-node serving the default and concentrated on coding-client integration, simpler gateway, local Mac deployments, and eventually verified coding tasks. Each transition followed an engineering constraint: restarts and weight transfers slowed distributed iteration; model-specific serving recipes did not travel cleanly across runtimes; compatible API did not always preserve an agents tool semantics; and long sessions depended on cache state outside the model. The challenge was to make those pieces work together, not merely find checkpoint that produced good text. Figure 1 summarizes the engineering layers that emerged during this journey. Figure 1: Conceptual overview of the engineering layers that verified coding work required, JulyOctober 2026: distributed inference across two laptops (Section 4), single-node serving with reproducible serving recipes (Section 5), coding-agent integration through thin gateway (Section 6), session continuity (Section 7) and task-specific behavioral verification (Section 9). The layers are shown in reading order, not strict chronology; in practice they overlapped. Client names are those tried during the work; tool icons are examples. For this report, models apparent progress can be separated into four levels: (1) served, meaning the checkpoint loads and responds; (2) coherent text, meaning it can answer in natural language; (3) parsed and executed tool calls, meaning its responses fit the agents interface; and (4) verified task completion, meaning the resulting code passes task-specific behavioral checks. These are not interchangeable. An endpoint can satisfy the first three while failing the fourth; an inability to satisfy the third may prevent me from measuring the fourth at all. Figure 2 shows these four levels and the boundaries at which progress can stop. Figure 2: The four success levels used in this report (Section 1) and where progress can stop. Artifact validation and parent review under the fixed artifact contract (Section 9.3) check form and interface (one JSON object, imports, exports and parameter signatures) before parent inspection and application; they are distinct from behavioral verification by task-specific hidden checks. The dashed band marks context, cached-prefix and session-affinity state, linked only to the serving runtime and the agent/gateway boundary (Section 7). Failure labels are engineering observations from Sections 59, not measured rates. The later delegation studies added further distinction. Working code is not yet verified outcome: in my delegation workflow, workers artifact also had to satisfy an interface contract and be accepted and applied by the parent before its hidden checks counted. running model, functional implementation, an accepted artifact and verified end-to-end coding outcome are therefore different things. The clearest illustration came from post-hoc diagnostic run after the experiments had closed (Section 9.4). selected the 36 valid-JSON worker artifacts that had been rejected solely for removing leading underscores from parameter names. With only that rule bypassed, 19 of the 36 passed the original hidden behavioral checks unchanged. They are not official successes or verified substitutions, because they never went through parent review and application. They do show that the design of an interface contract can reject functionally correct code before normal parent review begins. The diagnostic does not establish what any study would have scored without that rule. SWE-bench [1] and SWE-Lancer [2] motivate checking software outcomes instead of isolated snippets. Work on harness design and systems reliability [9, 11, 12] has already established the importance of the surrounding infrastructure. do not claim those general principles as novel. My contribution is concrete retrospective account of runtime/recipe constraints, counted operational failures, cache continuity, and bounded verified-task and delegation-economics studies. These are case studies at the end of the engineering journey, not summary of the entire project. The question throughout is: what had to work between an available open-weight checkpoint and code change developer could trust? 2. Scope: What Counts as Useful Work The report separates the engineering work of making coding agents operate from the bounded coding tasks evaluated with hidden behavioral checks. The former explains implementation choices and operational failures; the latter provides directly scored outcomes on selected TypeScript fixtures. Neither should be mistaken for representative evaluation of end-to-end software projects. 3 My target for local inference was working developer laptop, not machine cleared of other applications for peak-throughput benchmark. wanted model to run alongside Chrome, Cursor, Claude Code, an editor, terminals and ordinary development processes. This forced recurring choice: use the most capable model could fit, or preserve more memory for context, KV cache, other applications and responsive iteration. larger quantized checkpoint could appear to fit while leaving little room for long coding-agent conversation; smaller one could restore headroom at the potential cost of task capability. The relevant limit was not just the advertised maximum context or weight-file size, but how much context and performance remained practical under real workload. This was design objective and an observed constraint, not measurement of multitasking overhead. In the later Nemotron and Qwen studies, the machine was 32 GB Apple M1 Pro with substantial swap use, running one 4-bit 30B-class worker at time. Scope of small. In the title, small is practitioner-facing shorthand for models substantially smaller in active computation and deployment requirements than the frontier services used as reference. The primary tested worker here is 30B-total-parameter, approximately 3Bactive-parameter mixture-of-experts Qwen3-Coder checkpoint, with later studies of Nemotron Cascade 2 and Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B, both 4-bit MLX checkpoints of similar total and active scale. do not define all models below an arbitrary total-parameter threshold as equivalent, nor claim results for dense 3B models, 70B models, or every open-weight checkpoint configured. The terms small and smaller in this paper refer to these evaluated worker configurations unless explicitly noted otherwise. 3. Evidence, Workloads, and Boundaries 3.1 Where the observations came from This is retrospective account of my own work, pieced together from what saved along the way: configurations and code changes, integration-test results, inference logs, debugging conversations, and the results of the coding study. re-checked the reported counts against those saved results rather than re-running experiments. Throughout, distinguish operational measurements (timings and event counts), task-verified outcomes (results of hidden behavioral checks), implementation changes (what changed, not necessarily what improved), and engineering observations (problems encountered without an independent measurement). These records are private, so readers cannot check them directly; the Data availability statement describes what is and is not shared. These datasets have different units of observation and selection procedures; the preserved summary does not establish that the Gemma tool-request sample and debug-job sample are disjoint from, or exact subsets of, the gateway-turn population. The main sources of evidence were: Structured coding evaluation (45-trial study): 45 sessions across five TypeScript task categories and three execution conditions, scored using task-specific hidden behavioral tests separate from the coding agents own success claims (described in Section 9). Second task suite: 15 synthetic TypeScript repositories with sealed hidden checks. The Nemotron study paired 45 direct and 45 delegated sessions; separate Qwen follow-up ran 45 delegated sessions. Inputs, settings and model revisions were hash-recorded before scoring (Section 9.3). Additional task-level pilots: payment implementation, bounded fee and invoice tasks, twelve-adapter generation task, and earlier small-edit trials. Most individual cells have single run and are analyzed as case studies rather than statistically stable rates. Operational turns: 4,165 coding-agent turns logged by my gateway over three weeks in October 2026, spanning several model recipes. They include stop reasons, cache accounting, and TTFT on subset of turns. These are my own real working sessions, not an experimental assignment of prompts to models. Debug jobs: 623 unique jobs from selected saved debug sessions, predominantly Gemma 4 26B-A4B, including 85 narrowly defined cold-prefill records and 280 high-reuse records with performance metadata. Configuration and integration-test records: runtime settings, prompt-prefix rules, the models configured, and integration-test summaries for MLX, llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang. selected the models and workloads as practical problems arose, rather than assigning identical tasks randomly across systems. Some saved results also lack machine or runtime details. therefore use those records to explain engineering behavior, not to rank models by speed or reliability. Section 12 discusses the resulting limits. 3.2 What counts as result coding trial is verified when its task-specific hidden behavioral checks pass; these checks are separate from the coding agents own claims of success, not independently authored or externally audited tests. An artifact being emitted, proposed, inspected, or praised by the parent is not itself verification. successful substitution further requires the generated patch to be applied or retained rather than replaced by frontier-authored code. later check of the saved outputs found that all 26 verified delegation trials kept the worker-produced code. The harness alone does not prove that the frontier parent made no intermediate file edits through shell commands; therefore retained worker code must not be interpreted as no parent edits of any kind. This distinction matters: some pilots passed after the parent did not delegate, or without recorded apply event. In the later studies, verified substitution additionally required proposed worker artifact, parent inspection, confirmed application, passing sealed check, and no subsequent parent source rewrite. proposed artifact rejected by the parent is not substitution. Cost results use one measure throughout. API list-price-equivalent frontier cost is an estimate calculated from published API prices and the frontier models recorded token usage. It is not my actual subscription bill, and it excludes the unmeasured cost of running local workers. After this definition shorten it to frontier cost where the meaning is unambiguous; Section 10 gives the price assumptions. failed early stop can lower frontier cost without yielding useful software, and is never counted as saving. 4. The Early Detour: Splitting Inference Across Laptops My original aim was not limited to splitting 30B-class model between two laptops. wanted to know whether larger collection of everyday machines could jointly serve model that none could hold alone, potentially for colleagues on different networks. Avoiding special cables or shared physical setup was part of the hypothesis, not merely convenience: solution that depended on specialized connections would not support that distributed-team vision. began in late July with llama.cpp RPC, experimenting with local-network connections, tunnels, relay and WebRTC. Getting the leader and helper to communicate on macOS was difficult: inbound connections to the helpers RPC server failed or hung while outbound connections worked. made the helper dial out to the leader and used forwarding process with network access as another route; the precise macOS security mechanism was never confirmed. One early configuration also sent the helpers layers to its CPU instead of the Apple Silicon Metal device. corrected that device default, and later runs became more responsive, although the layer split changed too, preventing attribution to that correction alone. Once had working configuration, could use distributed inference over Wi-Fi for conversational chat. That was genuine feasibility milestone, but it did not settle whether the system was responsive enough for coding agent. The iteration loop was its own obstacle. In the RPC setup used, restarting after even small configuration change sent model data from the leader to the helper again: one saved 32B load transferred about 8.7 GB and took roughly five minutes over Wi-Fi. tried retaining and reattaching to live processes to avoid unnecessary reloads, and experimented with many layer allocations rather than assuming that an even division was best. Allocations derived from available memory sometimes placed most of the model on the remote helper. An even-looking layer allocation was not necessarily an even split of memory, computation or execution time, and each experiment involved another slow setup cycle. Some runs stalled or aborted; model transfers and responsiveness varied with the connection. Cache reuse appeared important during interactive use, but did not isolate its effect from networking. This changed the question was asking myself. If the model can answer over Wi-Fi, is that enough for developer agent that must make repeated model turns around tool calls? In my experience it was not. Chat felt usable, while coding-agent sessions remained too slow and cumbersome for productive work. In retrospect, wired Thunderbolt link might have been worth testing, but did not measure it against Wi-Fi. also explored splitting mixture-of-experts computation at the expert level, but did not establish usable configuration. The preserved record does not identify specific upstream defect, so cannot attribute that outcome to one. eventually parked the multi-machine direction and moved to one serving node at time so could make progress on the immediate coding-agent problem. That decision reflected the performance and development-loop costs of this particular implementation. It did not disprove distributed inference or the broader idea of pooling machines, and because no matched distributed-versus-single-node benchmark was preserved, it is not measured verdict on either. 5. One Model, Several Runtimes: Deployment Was Not Portable Once focused on single-node serving, the challenge shifted from distributing model to making deployment repeatable. moved through vLLM and SGLang on cloud GPUs, then returned to llama.cpp with GGUF checkpoints on Apple Silicon in October and added MLX later that month. The question was no longer just which combination could load checkpoint. Could turn that combination into dependable deployment, recreate it after machine change, and still sustain coding-agent session? Getting model running was not simply matter of downloading weights and starting server. encountered quantization and kernel incompatibilities, mismatched FlashInfer and Python dependencies, GPU driver problems, checkpoints larger than expected, context limits that werent passed through every layer, and runtime versions that needed specific pins. On one cloud configuration, an absent compiler prevented optimized attention kernels from building, so the runtime silently fell back to other kernels until the compiler and backend configuration were corrected; the surviving performance observation came from one engineering note. On another machine shape, the wrong GPU driver could lock up the host under CUDA load. checkpoint that 6 loaded under one engine sometimes needed different precision or revision under another. These differences complicated the one-command setup scripts was building. One launch path crashed because its generated shell script joined commands incorrectly; fixed the joining and added regression test for that malformed form. Worse, shared package-installation change intended for one model removed development headers another runtime required at boot. Existing instances continued running, but freshly created machines failed until the missing dependency was explicitly installed and fresh-startup regression test was added; an existing model-specific change rule was also extended to cover shared setup steps. The difficulties were therefore twofold: discovering working model-specific configuration and preserving it as repeatable installation rather than one-off manual success. On laptop, selecting the model was another deployment problem rather than simple preference for the largest checkpoint. Quantization reduced the space occupied by weights, but it did not eliminate memory used by the runtime, KV cache or concurrent applications. Mixture-of-experts models could have comparatively few active parameters while still carrying substantial resident weights. Long contexts also competed with free memory and prefill time. repeatedly had to choose between the potential ability of larger model and the usable context, responsiveness and headroom of smaller one. did not preserve controlled model-size-versus-context comparison, so these are trade-offs encountered, not measured optimum. The practical unit of deployment became checkpoint revision quantization runtime build parser/template context configuration agent client. successful recipe for one combination could not safely be copied to another, and an initially successful startup was not yet an operational deployment: the scripts also needed to reproduce the environment and expose the behavior that coding client expected. Supported did not mean interchangeable. Even after model loaded, still had to align its parser, reasoning format and tool schema with the coding client. That extra work is why came to treat deployment recipe, and not model name, as the unit of compatibility. Compatibility at the API level only made model reachable. Some models narrated command instead of calling tool, described planned action as prose, or rewrote function signature that should have remained stable. adjusted model recipes, prompts, delegation constraints and my expectations rather than trying to rewrite their behavior inside the gateway. These were practical adaptations, not tests of which prompt worked better, and behavioral portability still had to be established for each configuration. Table 1: Selected model/runtime integration findings Configuration GPT-OSS-120B / SGLang Laguna 2.1 / SGLang Integration finding Harmony tool parsing interacted with tool-choice settings; output limits could truncate tool-call JSON (configuration workaround; limited tests). checkpoint revision had to be pinned for the documented 96-GB GPU configuration (configuration record; no comparative experiment). 7 Configuration Laguna 2.1 / vLLM Qwen3.5-122B-A10B / SGLang Gemma 4 26B-A4B / MLX and llama.cpp Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B IQ3 / llama.cpp Nemotron Cascade 2 / MLX Integration finding missing compiler prevented FlashInfer JIT kernels from building and caused fallback to other kernels (dated configuration note; no retained trial series). thinking-budget processor serialization problem blocked startup until the implementation was adjusted (recorded fix; no verified coding score from this change). Template and parser anomalies appeared in saved requests; later cache cohorts span both runtimes (observational mixed-runtime records). Passed selected bounded coding tasks; tested context settings differed from the models native context length (task-verified outcomes). Selected bounded tasks succeeded or failed; some pilot worker records lack precise serving-artifact identification; the later scored study recorded fixed revision (bounded pilot results). These are selected integration cases, not ranking of runtimes or models; Sections 3 and 12 describe their evidence sources and limits. During an October llama.cpp upgrade, investigated tool-call parsing and cache-reuse concerns, then rolled back the change the next day. Both tool formatting and cache continuity mattered for the coding-agent workflow, but the surviving record does not establish specific regression caused by that upgrade. Dense and mixture-of-experts checkpoints further complicated deployment because their usable precision, memory footprint, kernels and runtime support differed. The practical question remained whether specific recipe could serve the model and support the client behavior required for coding. 6. From Text Responses to Tool-Using Coding Clients The client side changed as well. started with Cline, moved within days to OpenCode (and tried Kilo and Continue), and from September connected Claude Code through an Anthropic-compatible gateway. In those early weeks encountered malformed or text-only tool calls, mismatched thinking channels, tool loops and missing session identifiers. The symptoms differed enough that fixing one client or model combination rarely solved every other combination. At times, working with different checkpoints felt less like swapping libraries and more like collaborating with people who had markedly different habits. One model followed tool contract literally; another explained what it intended to do; another rewrote what it considered an awkward interface. do not mean that models are people or possess personalities. The analogy captures an engineering surprise: unlike exchanging one SDK implementation for another, using the same nominal API with different model did not guarantee the same behavior. That made evaluation and adaptation part of integration itself. 8 That prompted diagnostic question: when coding agent fails to use tool, did the model fail, or did the surrounding system lose the tool call on its way to execution? In August increasingly addressed incompatibilities at their source (model templates, parser rules, serve flags and request translation) instead of accumulating one-off output repairs. In September simplified the gateway toward thin translator, reducing the number of places where request or response could be altered. later gateway audit made that principle concrete: validation on the Claude path was restricted to protocol and security checks, while model-quality interventions were removed. also worked to propagate upstream failures as errors rather than letting failed stream appear to finish normally with an empty response. None of this proved that every failure was fixed; the actual client still had to be exercised end to end. To check the evolving translation layer before relying on the full coding client, exercised the gateway with Python API harness sending Anthropic Messages requests and Claude Code-style tools to Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on SGLang. The harness was not the Claude Code application. Successive synthetic-workspace checks returned different pass counts as the configurations evolved; the runs do not isolate the effect of single change. The preserved synthetic run sequence was 2/12; separate one-scenario 0/1; 10/12; 11/12; 12/12; and 12/12 passes. Separate existing-codebase checks returned 1/3 and, in later run with different task mix, 1/1. do not combine those results with the synthetic scores. The existing-codebase material remains conditional on the private-workload review in Section 12. The real Claude Code sessions then exposed problems that passing an API schema check had not eliminated. In one October episode, the clients working directory failed to reach the model-facing request, leaving the model to guess paths. In another, the gateway handled streamed tool-argument fragments as replacements instead of appending them. Both could derail an agent before the quality of its proposed code was even tested. They are individual debugging episodes, not frequency estimates. This changed how thought about compatibility: needed to test the client, translation layer, model template and tool execution as one path, including streamed arguments, stop behavior and session state. Several concrete cases illustrate where that path broke: GPT-OSS-120B SGLang path required coercing tool_choice=required to auto because the former interacted badly with Harmony tool parsing. The serving configuration also used higher output allowance on tool rounds to avoid truncating reasoning and tool JSON together. recorded soak passed tool suite while still encountering malformed arguments for task-list-management tool (todowrite) and plan-then-stop case. Gemma 4 saved outputs included eight distinct malformed <tool_call>callcall:-prefixed completions that produced no parsed tool call. The malformed completions illustrate parserboundary problem, not an overall agent-success rate. Three initially suspected leaked-token cases were excluded after detection-rule recheck found no matching events. Integration records distinguish recipes that are configured for runtime from those actually served and evaluated. model being configured is not evidence that it behaves correctly as an agent. The gateway records made the distinction between tool-protocol behavior and task completion particularly visible. The following are event counts from selected saved requests, not pass/fail rates: 9 Table 2: Observed tool and gateway events (distinct observational subsets) Source / denominator Recorded outcome Gemma requests containing tools (492 prompts) Gemma requests containing tools (492 prompts) Gateway turns with recorded timing (2,816 turns) Gateway turns with recorded timing (2,816 turns) Gateway turns with recorded timing (2,816 turns) Gateway turns with recorded timing (2,816 turns) Gateway turns with recorded timing (2,816 turns) Parsed outputs ending in tool_calls Outputs ending stop with no parsed tool call empty_content stream_failed repetition_cut job_failed Fallback flag Count 294 144 44 21 15 40 The 294 tool-call outcomes and 144 no-tool-call stop outcomes are selected recorded outcomes, not an exhaustive partition of the 492 prompts; the remaining 54 have no saved parsed response. stop without tool call can be an appropriate final response. Each timed gateway turn records at most one error class: the four listed error categories are disjoint (154 of 2,816 turns), with two rarer classes covering another three turns. Fallback is separate flag, and 19 of its 40 flagged turns also had empty_content. Without knowing what action each task required, neither these events nor the stop reasons establish coding success rates. What they do show is that generation, parsing and streaming can interrupt the agent before task correctness can be evaluated. Prior controlled work has likewise documented harness sensitivity and tool-interface effects [11, 12]. 7. Long Sessions: Context and Cache State Are Part of the Integration Getting individual tools to work did not mean long coding session would remain usable. The question became: why could conversation that looked continuous to the developer suddenly behave as though the model were starting over? Two forms of state became important: the clients evolving conversation and the runtimes cached token prefix. client or gateway that changes earlier messages, routes session to different slot, or inserts auxiliary work can destroy cache continuity without changing what the user thinks the conversation is about. Long coding-agent conversations often reuse large system prompt, tool schema and the growing history of tool calls and results. An effective inference backend can reuse cached key-value state for an identical token prefix, but application-layer prompt changes can silently defeat that reuse. 10 Practical changes in timestamps, system banners, tools, or JSON serialization may force expensive prefill. Compaction was separate long-session challenge. In private-workload integration exercise, deliberately lowered compaction thresholds in 12 OpenCode/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B tests. Sub-agent compaction triggered in six (main-session compaction never triggered), but none of those six sub-agent tasks completed; one recorded PASS label even contradicted the incomplete-task checks. That showed why could not treat compaction occurred as work completed. This example remains subject to the private-workload review in Section 12. 7.1 Gemma session observations Table 3: Gemma 4 26B-A4B requests from saved debug sessions (MLX and llama.cpp) Group definition Cold: no reused prefix (cache_n=0), 30k36k input tokens Warm: 90% reported reuse, <2k fresh tokens Unique jobs Median TTFT 85 280 69.4 2.8 These are selected, differently composed jobs rather than randomized or matched runs; the timings do not isolate the effect of caching. Among the 85 cold jobs, 54 fell between 65 and 82 seconds; 59 of the cold jobs are attributed to llama.cpp. Of 280 warm jobs, 167 are attributed to llama.cpp. The remaining 26 cold and 113 warm jobs are attributed to MLX in the saved runtime breakdown. In warm jobs that recorded decode throughput, the median was 38.5 tokens/s across 206 records. Some selected warm requests had TTFT near one second. 7.2 Broader gateway-turn observations Table 4: Selected gateway turns, not controlled model comparisons Recipe Warm group (n), median TTFT Cold group (n), median TTFT Gemma 4 26B-A4B Nemotron Cascade 2 Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B IQ3 1,128; 3.0 338; 10.8 282; 2.0 259; 67.0 90; 86.6 29; 135.6 In Table 4, warm means at least 8,000 reused prefix tokens (cache_n >= 8000), and cold means none (cache_n == 0). These definitions differ from Table 3, where the warm group requires at least 90% reported reuse and fewer than 2,000 fresh tokens, while the cold group has no reused prefix and 30,00036,000 input tokens. The model recipes were used under different request mixes, and machine provenance is incomplete. The numbers show substantial observed difference associated with prefix-cache state; they do not rank model speed or show that any local patch caused the difference. 11 7.3 Application-layer cache discipline For sessions intended to reuse an exact cached token prefix, treated the model-facing message sequence as append-only where practical, except when genuine context changes required rewriting earlier content. Earlier tool messages should not be cosmetically re-serialized; streamed and final tool call JSON must match; per-turn metadata should not modify the frozen system prefix; and MLX cache fingerprints should include each rendering input that genuinely affects output tokens while excluding irrelevant changing fields. Restoring hybrid sliding-window attention state from llama.cpp slot checkpoints also proved awkward, so added local handling for restoration. One recorded restore-related slow case took approximately 70 seconds. have no matched post-change timing; the immediate engineering goal was to get the interrupted session back into usable state. 7.4 Auxiliary requests and session affinity Coding-agent traffic includes auxiliary requests, such as title generation or permission-related operations, in addition to the main coding conversation. In an inference setup with single reusable execution slot, an auxiliary request may replace the main conversations resident prompt state. The subsequent coding turn can then require renewed prefill, even if the main conversation itself maintained stable prefix. In the saved debug sessions, 65 requests were classified as auxiliary; 44 of these recorded no cached-prefix reuse. Among the available high-reuse timing records, auxiliary requests had median TTFT of about 12.2 seconds (13 observations), compared with about 2.7 seconds for main requests (267 observations). These are differently composed observational groups, not an estimate of the latency caused by auxiliary requests or proof of particular eviction event in each case. Session affinity was the other half of the problem. stable prompt does little good if the next turn reaches an execution slot without its cached state. Because clients did not always supply usable session identifier, added session-affinity and slot-handling logic. The records do not isolate speed gain from that change, but it led me to practical design principle: preserve both the token prefix and the route to compatible cache state. These findings complement established prefix/cache mechanisms such as vLLMs PagedAttention [3] and SGLangs RadixAttention [4]. The concern here is the applicationruntime boundary: even sophisticated cache cannot reuse prefix that an upstream agent gateway changes unnecessarily. 8. When the Protocol Worked, Coding Could Still Fail Once tool requests could pass through the gateway, harder question remained: what counts as completing the coding work: producing patch, type-checking it, or showing that it meets the requested behavior? encountered different class of failure: the agent could appear to make progress without completing the intended change. In October sessions, models sometimes described shell command instead of invoking it, narrated the tool they wanted to use, or reproduced long file path with characters missing. Those were observed interactions, not measured rates. Repository understanding was another failure point. In one September Claude Code session, the agent re-implemented functionality that already existed and left state that was never updated, even though type checking did not flag the problem. This example survives only as contemporaneous account, not saved execution artifacts, and remains subject to the Section 12 12 private-workload review. It illustrates why valid tool call and successful type check need not imply the requested behavior was implemented. Another failure class involved artifacts and repository contracts. In bounded invoice attempt, Nemotron Cascade 2 worker artifact failed export-preservation validation. The delegation tool returned malformed before the parent inspected, applied or tested any worker code; the saved status does not identify which missing declaration triggered the check. That is rejected artifact, not failed invoice behavioral test. In separate payment pilots, outputs sometimes changed public function signatures (for example, replacing export function declarations with arrow-function constants), while the separate parent constraint list was not forwarded to the worker in that period. Another Nemotron attempt produced malformed JSON before any valid patch could be assessed. Execution limits could prevent evaluation altogether. twelve-adapter Nemotron Cascade 2 worker request stopped after approximately 120 seconds with an unavailable/http result, produced no candidate implementation and left the stub untouched. The direct version completed, but its estimated visible code length fell below the tasks intended 2,500-token threshold for testing larger generated-code workload. This episode illustrates the effect of timeout and workload boundaries on what can be evaluated, not an established inability of the worker to implement the task. Finally, passing scorer is not the same as attributing the code to worker. In payments pilot, voluntarily delegated arm passed despite zero recorded delegation events; another scorer-passing pilot had no recorded inspect/apply events. Neither establishes verified worker substitution on its own. Across these failure types, tracing the broken layer mattered as much as obtaining candidate code, consistent with the broader systems view in [9]. 9. Case Study: Coding Tasks with Hidden Behavioral Verification used Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 as the fixed parent harness throughout these delegation studies. It was the client had integrated most deeply, and holding it fixed let me examine worker behavior and delegation overhead within an actual workflow. OpenCode and other harnesses might behave differently; did not test them as interchangeable parents, and these findings are about the tested system, not harness-independent model capability. The engineering journey eventually reached more controlled question: after the deployment, tool and session problems had been addressed well enough to run bounded work, could an open-weight worker produce code that passed task-specific checks? The later 45-trial evaluation is my first repeated coding outcome dataset. treat it as case study within the July-to-October integration work, not as its central explanation. Study design. The evaluation covered five TypeScript task categories (quote, prorate, customer, split, parts), three conditions, three trials per category and condition, totaling 45 sessions. The conditions were direct frontier execution, optimized delegation, and batch-labeled adaptive delegation. Task-specific hidden behavioral scorers, separate from the agents own success claims, determined verification. The harness uses Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B IQ3 worker in the delegation conditions, with Claude Opus 5.5 as the parent/frontier model. In this earlier study, the worker received the artifact contract, task text and supplied file context, but the parents separate constraints field was not forwarded. gateway path also dropped duplicate system message and truncated messages above 1,800 characters. Of 41 reconstructed worker prompts, two lost approximately 220 final 13 characters; both belonged to failed trials. None of the verified trials had reconstructed first-attempt prompt over the limit, although one retry prompt could only be estimated. These observations leave the frozen outcomes unchanged but limit interpretation of instruction-following failures. In the optimized condition, the parent was instructed to delegate bounded implementation and apply worker artifacts rather than write implementation code itself. In the batch-labeled condition, the parent was likewise instructed to apply worker artifacts rather than independently write the implementation; it could divide work into sequential worker packages when it judged task parts independent, or fall back to single delegation for coupled changes. Only 5/15 batch-labeled trials actually used batch call (three packages each); the remaining 10/15 used one delegation. Among the 14 verified batch-labeled trials, five used batch calls and nine used single delegation. Consequently, this condition is an adaptive prompting-and-delegation policy, not clean experimental comparison of batching versus non-batching. These are the studys own condition names, not standardized algorithms; worker packages were not executed concurrently. 9.1 Multi-trial comparison Table 5: Structured coding-task verification (five task categories, three trials per category per arm) Execution condition Direct frontier coding Optimized frontier open-weight delegation Batch-labeled adaptive delegation Verified trials Total trials 95% Wilson interval Interpretation 15 12 15 [0.80, 1.00] 15 [0.55, 0.93] Every trial passed the task-specific hidden behavioral scorer. Three trials failed verification. [0.70, 0.99] One trial failed verification. All 26 verified delegated trials retained worker-produced implementations, although the harness does not rule out intermediate parent edits. These are successes on the selected fixtures, not separate applications. The Wilson intervals overlap; because the 15 trials per condition repeat only five task categories, these run-level intervals should not be interpreted as uncertainty across independent new coding tasks. With three runs per task/condition cell and one worker configuration, the data do not establish general success-rate differences. The frontier-cost consequences are analyzed separately in Section 10. 9.2 Verified worker contributions Verified worker contributions were not limited to the later 45-trial study. Earlier small-task experiments also produced retained worker code, although they are less conclusive than the repeated evaluation. three-task comparison of two delegation arrangements reported 3/3 verified with retained worker code for the newer arrangement and 0/3 for the earlier arrangement; the saved summary does not sufficiently characterize their differences to isolate mechanism. Separately, three worker runs from the earlier small-edit trials passed hidden checks on the same three task types; these are separate executions, not six distinct task types. These single-run observations point to the importance of orchestration, but cannot establish which architectural change mattered. later bounded fee task using Nemotron Cascade 2 also produced task-verified open-weight implementation that was applied to the task codebase. The fee example is one later, separate case study, not the only successful worker substitution across the project. 9.3 Second Task Suite Under Fixed Artifact Contract later prepared second suite of 15 synthetic TypeScript repositories, three each involving bug fixes, features, multi-file integrations, export-preserving refactors and test-driven repairs, with sealed hidden checks. The fixed artifact contract was derived from my practical delegation setup; this was not trial on production repositories. Each original stub failed its check and each reference solution passed. These tasks and checks were developed with AI assistance and hash-recorded before the scored sessions. The worker contract was fixed before scoring: one delegation attempt, 120-second worker deadline, 4,096 output tokens, temperature 0, 32,768 model context and 24,000-character supplied-file gate. The locally served models used MLX on the 32 GB laptop. An artifact had to be one JSON object, satisfy static checks on imports, exports and exported function parameter lists, and pass parent inspection before application. passing sealed check without worker application was not verified substitution. The Nemotron study paired three direct and three Nemotron Cascade 2 delegated repetitions for each task (90 sessions) on frozen schedule. The Qwen follow-up used the same tasks and fixed artifact contract for 45 later delegated sessions with Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B, but no new direct arm. These cohorts were not contemporaneous or randomized together: the Qwen sessions ran later, and the parents prompt-cache state was not reset between studies. The earlier Qwen IQ3/llama.cpp study used different tasks and should not be pooled with them. The direct arm passed all three repetitions of every task. The Qwen follow-up passed none. Nemotron yielded 11 verified substitutions, plus one session verified after the parent rewrote source code; these are different outcomes. Qwen yielded no verified substitutions. Crucially, 13 proposed artifacts (8 Nemotron, 5 Qwen) were rejected by the parent after inspection, not applied and then failed by the hidden tests. separate Nemotron proposal went unreviewed when the parents subscription spend limit interrupted the session. The sealed check in these cases ran on unchanged repositories. Thus artifact production, parent acceptance and functional verification must remain separate stages. Because all 15 Qwen task means are zero, the computed Student-t interval is [0, 0]. This is degenerate property of the observed task means, not evidence that the underlying chance of success 16 is zero. Repetitions are also clustered within tasks and should not be treated as 45 independent task draws. There was procedural deviation in the Nemotron study: 16 scheduled sessions rejected by subscription spend limit before any model call were excluded and replaced by fresh executions following plan change, contrary to the written protocols instruction to retain every scheduled session. An earlier session stopped after worker proposal and remained failure rather than being rerun. The replacements affected the reported outcomes: eight Nemotron reruns contributed four of its 12 verified sessions, including three of its 11 substitutions; eight direct reruns contributed eight of the 45 direct successes. If the 16 original pre-inference rejections were instead counted as failures under the written keep-all-sessions rule, direct coding would be 37/45, Nemotron verification 8/45 and Nemotron substitutions 8/45. These alternative counts describe scheduled-workflow interruptions, not additional model-inference failures. The principal results describe the completed replacement cohort, with the deviation and its effect disclosed. Figure 3 summarizes the verified outcomes and frontier cost across the three separate studies. Figure 3: Verified outcomes and API list-price-equivalent frontier cost in the three delegation studies, each with Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code as the parent. (A) The 45-trial study. (B) The Nemotron study and (C) the Qwen follow-up, on separate 15-task suite under the fixed artifact contract. Panels use different tasks, workers, runtimes and dates and are not pooled. Panel (B) reports the completed replacement cohort; Nemotrons 12 verified sessions comprise 11 verified worker substitutions and one session verified after parent source rewrite. The keep-all sensitivity (37/45 direct, 8/45 Nemotron) is given in Section 9.3. In (C) no session was verified, so cost per verified success is undefined. Costs include failed sessions; local worker cost was not measured. 17 9.4 When the Interface Rejects Correct Code The signature validator compared the text of existing exported function parameter lists, including parameter names. Stubs often prefixed unused parameters with an underscore (_entries); workers sometimes removed that underscore when implementing the function (entries). Ordinary positional callers do not depend on this spelling, but the contracts strict signature rule rejected the artifact before parent review. This was compliance with the written contract, not demonstrated parsing bug. After both studies were closed, ran post-hoc offline diagnostic, without new model inference or code repair. selected the 36 valid-JSON artifacts rejected solely for dropping leading underscores (23 Qwen, 13 Nemotron), applied each unchanged to fresh task copy while bypassing only that name-comparison rule, and ran the original sealed checks. Three other Qwen signature rejections changed more than the underscores and were excluded. All 15 baseline tasks failed their checks and all 15 reference implementations passed. Table 5d: Post-hoc signature sensitivity (selected rejected artifacts; not scored successes) Worker Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B Nemotron Cascade 2 Total Underscore-only rejections Pass sealed check unchanged Still fail behaviorally 13 36 12 7 19 6 17 The diagnostic identified 19 functionally passing artifacts that the original interface gate had rejected, the observation previewed in Section 1. On some tasks every artifact in this selected class passed; on others, removing the gate exposed incorrect numeric results, thrown errors, ordering mistakes or missed edge cases. The rule screened out both useful and incorrect output. These offline passes are not verified substitutions or counterfactual end-to-end successes: the artifacts never entered normal parent inspection and application. The frozen scores remain Qwen 0/45 and Nemotron 12/45. This narrower result demonstrates how static contract can suppress functionally passing code without establishing model-capability ranking or what the parent would have accepted. Figure 4 illustrates how interface-contract rejection differs from behavioral failure, including the selected post-hoc diagnostic. 18 Figure 4: Delegated-session outcomes under the fixed artifact contract and an offline diagnostic of one validation rule. (A) Scored outcomes (Table 5c): verified worker substitutions, sessions verified after parent source rewrite, and their totals. (B) An illustrative example, not taken from specific task, of the strict signature rule rejecting an artifact whose parameter name lost its leading underscore. (C) Post-hoc diagnostic (Section 9.4, Table 5d): the 36 valid-JSON artifacts rejected solely for dropped leading underscores were applied unchanged with only that rule bypassed, and 19 passed the same sealed hidden checks. These are not verified substitutions: the artifacts never entered parent inspection or application, and the scored results remain 12/45 (Nemotron) and 0/45 (Qwen). Three other Qwen signature rejections that changed more than the underscores were excluded. Among Qwens 45 scored sessions, only 12 saved artifacts passed the post-hoc behavioral checks unchanged after the underscore-only rule was bypassed. Thus, relaxing only that rule, without repairing other artifacts, could have made at most 12 of those existing artifacts behaviorally passing candidates for further parent review. This is not projection of 12 verified substitutions: parent acceptance, application and end-to-end verification were not replayed. Nor does it show that Qwens remaining sessions reflect fixed capability limits; other interventions, such as the bounded repair attempt proposed in Section 11, were not tested. 10. Case Study: The Cost of Delegating Implementation The workflow tested question that had become more concrete after the integration work: if smaller model can produce code that passes verification, does delegating that work actually save anything? strong parent model reads repository and delegates bounded implementation to an inexpensive local worker; the parent inspects and applies only suitable artifacts. Intuitively this 19 could replace costly frontier output tokens with local generation. But the parent must communicate requirements, preserve constraints, inspect candidate artifacts, and potentially recover from failures. For task, define: Cdirect = Cfrontier,direct Cdelegate = Cparent,context + Cspec + Creview + Crecovery + Cworker The equations describe conceptual full-cost comparison. The study measured the frontier terms only; local worker expenditure was unmeasured and must not be treated as zero. For repeated workload, compare observed frontier cost per task-verified success in this study, not merely cost per request or cost for failed attempts that ended early. priced the structured study using the study-era Claude Opus 5.5 list rates: $4 per million uncached input tokens, $0.20 per million cache-read tokens, $5 per million five-minute cache-write tokens, $8 per million one-hour cache-write tokens, and $20 per million output tokens. The accounting distinguishes those token classes; thinking tokens are included in output and are not charged twice. Each cache-write token was priced using its recorded five-minute or one-hour cache lifetime (predominantly one-hour). The resulting per-trial totals matched the clients reported list-price cost estimates across all 45 trials. These are historical study assumptions, not current vendor prices. All reported frontier costs are API list-price equivalents based on recorded usage, not per-token amounts paid: the frontier sessions ran under personal Claude subscription. Across the five structured task categories, direct execution had the lowest measured frontier cost per verified success  (Table 6)  . The amounts below include the frontier cost of failed trials in the numerator; verification counts appear in parentheses. Table 6: API list-price-equivalent frontier cost per verified success by task category (USD) Task category quote prorate customer split parts All categories Direct Optimized delegation Batch-labeled delegation $0.142 (3/3) $0.126 (3/3) $0.156 (3/3) $0.117 (3/3) $0.140 (3/3) $0.136 (15/15) $0.249 (2/3) $0.512 (1/3) $0.204 (3/3) $0.153 (3/3) $0.163 (3/3) $0.214 (12/15) $0.300 (2/3) $0.179 (3/3) $0.210 (3/3) $0.157 (3/3) $0.185 (3/3) $0.199 (14/15) Each value is the total API list-price-equivalent frontier cost for its trials, including failed trials, divided by the number verified; parentheses show verified/total. Each task-category cell has only three trials, and the optimized prorate figure rests on one verified success. These are descriptive figures, not general performance estimates. Direct execution also had the lowest mean frontier cost per trial in each category, so the directional result does not depend on penalizing failed attempts. The separate fee pilot illustrates the distinction between successful substitution and savings: its worker implementation passed and was applied, but 20 the frontier cost was $0.1856 with delegation versus $0.1293 directly, and recorded wall time, which includes local worker execution, was 126.4 seconds versus 27.4 seconds. These figures describe that one case. The second task suite strengthens this economic observation without making it general claim about model cascades. Table 7: API list-price-equivalent frontier cost on the second task suite (USD) Total API list-price equivalent $6.888 $15.761 Per session $0. $0.350 Per verified success Per verified substitution $0.153 $1.313 n/a $1.433 $16.023 $0.356 Undefined (0 verified) Undefined Condition Nemotron study: direct Nemotron study: delegation Qwen follow-up: delegation The Nemotron delegation arrangement consumed roughly 8.6 times the direct frontier cost per verified success. Failures are included in the spending numerator. Qwens per-success amount is undefined rather than zero. Neither table measures local worker electricity, hardware, depreciation or engineering time. Table 7 reports the completed replacement cohort; the keep-all sensitivity in Section 9.3 gives alternative outcome counts, not separate cost calculation. The result illustrates practical economic tension: reducing frontier implementation tokens does not guarantee lower frontier cost if specifying, reviewing and recovering delegated work uses additional parent tokens. The records cannot apportion those overheads cleanly into separate orchestration and review effects. The finding applies to the selected tasks, study-era parent pricing, worker configuration and delegation contract. This result does not refute cascades or model routing in general. Prior work examines cost-aware model selection [5], and Scrouting [13] provides positive counterexample: small repository-scouting model followed by routed frontier fixers solved 159 of 266 tasks versus 158 for the strongest single fixer, at approximately one fifth of its reported cost per solve. Its small-model-scouts/frontiermodel-fixes direction is the reverse of my frontier-specifies/local-model-implements contract. therefore limit the negative cost finding to the measured delegation arrangement and do not generalize it to all routing or cascades. An architecture with substantially different task boundaries or large mechanically generated artifact might behave differently, but my data cannot establish that counterfactual. 11. Practical Lessons Across the Journey The journey suggests five practical rules. They are not new universal principles; they emerge from trying to make the components work in one evolving setup and from the bounded studies reported here. 21 First, define success at the task boundary. Serving checkpoint, obtaining coherent answer, executing parsed tools, and producing verified code are distinct milestones. Test the actual client and the resulting behavior, rather than trusting plausible response or harnesss own PASS label. Second, treat deployment as full recipe and model selection as workload decision. Checkpoint revision, quantization, runtime, template, context, gateway, client and resident memory all matter. On working laptop could choose larger, potentially stronger model or leave more room for KV cache, useful context and the applications needed to do my work. The best name on leaderboard was not necessarily the best workable configuration for that afternoon. Third, make session continuity an application-level responsibility. Keep prefixes stable where possible, preserve affinity to reusable cache state and account for auxiliary requests. The developer can see one continuous conversation while the runtime incurs costly new prefill. Fourth, evaluate delegation per verified outcome. Count worker-produced code separately from verified application, price the parent specification, inspection and recovery, and include failed attempts. The observed delegation arrangements retained useful open-weight contributions, but in the two studies with direct arm, delegation did not reduce measured frontier cost per verified success. Fifth, verify artifacts by behavior when practical. Cheap static gates have purpose, yet contract stricter than the behavior the application needs can exclude passing code. Parent acceptance is another separate filter. The post-hoc test did not replace the frozen scores; it exposed why malformed label alone does not mean the implementation was behaviorally wrong. follow-up have not run. The signature diagnostic points to one concrete next experiment, which this report does not include. Under the same fixed contract, worker whose artifact fails validation would receive the specific validation error and be allowed one bounded repair attempt. The study would measure artifact acceptance, genuine verified worker substitutions, overall task verification, the additional worker time and inference cost, and frontier cost per verified success with unsuccessful attempts included. repair turn might recover some contract-rejected work, but it also adds parent and worker turns, so it may not improve verification or reduce cost; only run with the same accounting could show which effect dominates. Beyond the rules. Working with larger cloud-hosted models sometimes felt different in reasoning and agent behavior, but that was my impression, not matched comparison. Those checkpoints, many of them mixture-of-experts, were used with different machines, runtimes and clients; cannot infer model-size threshold, including one at 70B parameters, or rank dense and MoE architectures. Larger dense checkpoints raise distinct practical resource burden on everyday developer hardware, while active-parameter counts alone can obscure the weight-memory burden of an MoE model. The unfavorable economics should not obscure the value obtained from open weights. could inspect and modify checkpoint choices, quantization, runtime builds, templates, parsers, cache behavior and routing rather than wait for providers implementation. In the first study, 26 of 30 delegated trials retained verified worker code; in the Nemotron study, 11 of 45 were verified worker substitutions under the stricter contract. Those are bounded but real achievements. Useful local work and lower frontier expenditure proved to be different questions. 22 12. Limitations and Evidence Quality Evidence classes are not interchangeable. recorded change shows that something was changed, not what it achieved. test scripts PASS verdict shows what that script reported, not independent correctness. Notes written at the time describe what saw but cannot replace saved task artifacts. The report follows my evolving workloads and is not reproducible controlled comparison across runtimes or clients. Private-workload boundaries. Some integration tests and one observed session used an existing private codebase. They are presented, where used, only as generic aggregate or qualitative experience; no source code, prompts, paths or identifiers are disclosed. Their use remains subject to the authors publication-permission review, and the entire narrative remains supportable from synthetic cases, October logs and verified task records if those observations must be removed. Distributed-phase measurements. have records of what built and decided during the early multi-machine phase but no matched throughput or latency measurements that would justify numerical performance claims. AI-assisted task and scorer development. The author reports that Claude or another AI assistant contributed to drafting the five task definitions and hidden tests. The combined harness file was created about 39 seconds before the first evaluated session and first saved to version control after the last of the 45 sessions. Task instructions and visible checks were identical in all 45 saved runs, and recorded score labels agree with the scorer as later saved. However, no independently preserved pre-run snapshot of the hidden-test implementation is available. Changes to hidden scoring logic between file creation and that later save cannot be ruled out. The precise AI tool and extent of human review have not been recovered. The study was not preregistered, and these uncertainties limit claims about benchmark independence. The second suite was also developed with AI assistance, but its tasks, hidden checks, worker settings and model revisions were frozen and hash-recorded before scoring. Author-operated session provenance. The author confirms that the 4,165 gateway turns came exclusively from the authors own research sessions, not other users sessions. This is retrospective convenience sample of the authors work, not representative production-user cohort. Personal operation of the sessions does not remove possible third-party or confidential information embedded in prompts, source excerpts, and tool results. Only aggregate results are reported. Limited task diversity. The multi-trial benchmark covered five selected TypeScript tasks. Additional pilots are one-off fixtures. My data lack controlled set of real website-building or broadly representative software projects. Claims about full-product development would be unjustified. No front-end design metric. The verified coding tasks do not include validated visual-design, end-user usability, or full-product experience metric. Real coding work refers to the agent integration experience and bounded task-checked implementations, not broad assessment of complete application quality. Limited worker diversity in verified tasks. The initial study used one Qwen IQ3/llama.cpp worker configuration. The later suite used Nemotron and Qwen MLX 4-bit configurations on different days. Other models configured were not evaluated with comparable hidden checks, and this does not establish cross-family coding rankings. Fixed parent harness and later-study design. All delegation studies used Claude Code with 23 Claude Opus 5.5 as parent. Other harnesses such as OpenCode were not tested as parents and might specify, inspect and recover differently. The later studies ran at different times on one laptop without resetting the parents prompt cache. Sixteen spend-limit rejections before inference were replaced contrary to the written keep-all-sessions rule; keeping those pre-inference rejections as failures would give direct coding 37/45 and Nemotron 8/45 verified (8 substitutions), rather than the reported replacement-cohort 45/45 and 12/45. One interrupted post-proposal session was retained as failure. The Claude Code client version also changed during Nemotron execution. These circumstances limit causal comparisons. Earlier worker inputs and retrospective sensitivity. In the 45-trial study, the worker did not receive the parents separately provided constraint list; two reconstructed worker prompts were truncated at 1,800 characters. Both were in failing trials. The later underscore-relaxation check selected rejected artifacts after the fact, bypassed one validation gate and did not replay parent review or application. It is diagnostic, not revised operational score. Nonrandomized observational data. Gateway turns and debug sessions were saved selectively during engineering. Cold and warm cache cohorts differ in evaluated prefix work and may differ in other aspects. TTFT differences are descriptive rather than causal. Incomplete hardware and runtime metadata. Some source files lack machine field, exact artifact version, or runtime version. Machine details recovered later cannot be reliably matched to individual saved trials. This prevents hardware-normalized inference comparisons. Available memory and background application activity were not logged consistently, so the developer-workstation objective should not be interpreted as controlled test of multitasking performance. Price accounting scope. The cost tables report API list-price-equivalent frontier cost by token/cache category, not amounts invoiced. Hardware, engineering time, energy, and depreciation were not measured. Hence cheaper refers only to the specified API list-price-equivalent frontier-cost comparison. Evidence corrections and missing records. One fee-substitution attribution was corrected after the run, and both versions were kept. Some original Nemotron debug details were lost; unrecoverable fields must remain unknown. The original result files were marked as non-official evaluation records and should not be recast as preregistered official study. No causal evaluation of cache changes. Engineering rules describe how to protect exact-prefix reuse, and traffic shows striking cold/warm differences, but the evidence does not directly quantify the causal benefit of each patch. 13. Related Work SWE-bench [1] established repository-level issue resolution as more realistic coding evaluation than function synthesis, and SWE-Lancer [2] connected software tasks to economic value and independent end-to-end checking. This report extends neither dataset. Instead it studies operational and economic conditions surrounding smaller, self-hosted workers, under its own much narrower tasks. In inference systems, vLLM and PagedAttention [3] address efficient KV memory management; SGLang [4] describes structured LM execution and RadixAttention-based prefix reuse. This report does not claim either caching method as original. It documents application-layer prompt-stability difficulties and operational latency associated with cache state in long agent sessions. Cost-aware 24 model cascades such as FrugalGPT [5] provide conceptual context; supervised code delegation workflow is distinct accounting unit because the parent still constructs specification and verifies the artifact. Recent research closely overlaps with parts of this study. Jarmak [9] synthesizes evidence that codingagent outcomes depend on reliability chain extending well beyond the model, while Harness-Bench [11] and Fan et al. [12] experimentally document harness sensitivity and tool-interface effects. do not claim those general conclusions as new. non-peer-reviewed single-H100 report by serbulent-av [10] evaluates Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B in agentic coding. Its plan-once and review-loop experiments also underscore that orchestration choices interact with the worker and test setup; those pilots did not evaluate the same delegation contract or frontier-cost accounting used here. Its single-H100 results should not be conflated with its separate multi-GPU (8 H200) evaluation. Peng, Lin, and Lee [6] examine cloud versus on-premise coding-agent economics in nonrandomized longitudinal case study. Their cache-intensive frontier API configuration was economical per token; their proposed hybrid routing gateway was evaluated by offline simulation rather than execution. By contrast, my narrower structured study executed frontier-parent/local-worker delegation contract and accounted for the parent models frontier cost per task-verified outcome, though not local hardware cost. Scrouting [13] reports positive but reverse-direction routing design, making clear why my negative result should not be interpreted as rejection of cascades generally. Ariño de la Rubia and Pafka [7] find substantial run-to-run variability across open-weight agent configurations and cache-sensitive cost differences across much larger repeated-run study; their results underscore the limited precision of my three-trial cells. Nixon and colleagues [8] report strong results for local open-weight agents in governance-restricted research-data-preparation setting; their evaluation is restricted to that domain. Relative to these studies, my contribution is an evidence-qualified account of (1) model/runtime and coding-client interoperability across July-to-October engineering journey, (2) application/runtime cache and version-management observations from self-hosted inference, and (3) counted gateway and protocol failure events, complemented by (4) verified delegation across two task suites and three open-weight worker configurations from two model families, with separate accounting for validation, parent review and frontier spending. The contribution is the combined engineering account and its bounded studies, rather than new general-purpose benchmark. 14. Conclusion The central lesson of this engineering journey was the distance between running an open-weight model and reliably getting software work done through coding agent. started by trying to share inference across ordinary machines. learned to make deployments repeatable, tool calls executable and sessions less fragile, and finally to ask whether the code left behind actually passed independent checks. The same nominal API could hide different model behaviors, runtime states and interface failures. Neither successful startup nor persuasive explanation was enough. The structured studies gave bounded but encouraging answer to the titles question: yes, openweight workers produced verified coding contributions, including 26 retained-code successes in 30 delegated trials in the first study and 11 verified substitutions in 45 Nemotron delegated sessions under stricter contract. They also exposed real limits. Under that contract Qwen recorded no end-to-end verified success; parent review rejected additional proposals; static name-preservation rule rejected 19 artifacts that passed the original hidden checks when applied unchanged offline. In 25 the two studies with direct arm, direct frontier execution had the lower measured frontier cost per verified result. These are properties of the tested combinations, not final verdicts on the models or on delegation itself. Despite those difficulties, finish more optimistic about open-weight AI than when began. Over roughly three months of hands-on work, saw new capabilities, improvements in runtimes and tooling, and recurring integration problems become easier to understand or address. Those observations do not establish measured rate of industry-wide progress, and the path was rarely linear. Yet the direction felt increasingly promising: the distance between model that runs and system that does useful work became more tangible and, in places, more manageable. That progress rests on remarkable shared effort: researchers releasing open weights, engineers improving kernels and serving systems, maintainers fixing templates and runtime incompatibilities, and contributors to projects such as llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM and SGLang. Much of their work is invisible in benchmark tables, but encountered its value daily. am grateful to the people making these systems accessible, inspectable and improvable. This report records the difficulties of one moment in that progress, not permanent boundary. The gap between generating code and delivering trustworthy work remains substantial; the reason for optimism is how much thoughtful work is going into closing it.

sections.title: Statements and data availability
sections.content: Data availability. The underlying research records are privately preserved and are not part of this publication. No raw gateway logs, coding-agent or Cursor transcripts, prompts, model responses, source code (including harness code), deployment configurations, debug archives, evidence manifests, benchmark result files, task fixtures, hidden tests, scorers, or other raw research artifacts are publicly released or offered on request. The paper reports aggregated results and describes the methodology where possible, but independent reproduction and audit are limited by the restricted availability of the underlying records. sanitized subset of the synthetic fixtures, evaluation checks and aggregate results may be made available following privacy, intellectual-property and publication-permission review. No public release is currently authorized. Use of AI-assisted tools. AI-assisted tools were used in developing portions of the experimental harness, auditing evidence, checking reported statistics, and preparing and reviewing this manuscript. The author directed the research, evaluated the evidence, and takes responsibility for the reported findings and conclusions. Competing interests. The author is developing self-hosted AI infrastructure with potential commercial applications. The experimental system examined in this report is related to that work. Computing support. Computing resources were supported in part by Google Cloud Free Trial credits.
